title: SLO Exception and Temporary Mitigation Playbook
author: Aisha Tan
content:
Overview:

This playbook defines the SLO Exception Request (SER) lifecycle and the approved temporary mitigation patterns that on-call operators and service owners can use to limit customer impact while a root cause is investigated and a durable fix is implemented. It is intended for: service owners, on-call operators, incident commanders, capacity and SRE teams, and customer success for external communications.

Goals:
- Provide a fast, auditable path for temporarily relaxing or protecting SLOs under controlled conditions.
- Standardize mitigation actions (rate-limits, routing fallbacks, capacity isolation) with safe defaults and rollback gates.
- Ensure clear approval boundaries, evidence capture, and follow-up (post-incident actions).

When to use this playbook:
1) Sustained SLO degradation observed (>= 5 minutes) that is not resolved by immediate remediation.
2) Evidence shows broad customer impact or risk of cascading failures.
3) Temporary mitigation would reduce customer-visible errors or allow graceful degradation without permanent configuration change.

SLO Exception Request (SER) quick checklist:
- Trigger: SLO breach or immediate risk of breach.
- Owner: service owner or primary on-call (must submit request).
- Approver: On-call tech lead for P1/P2; Service SLA manager + Eng director for P0 or regulatory-facing services.
- Max Exception Duration: 72 hours by default (can be extended to 7 days with Exec approval).
- Required artifacts: monitoring evidence (graphs, trace ids), mitigation plan, rollback plan, customer comm draft.

SLO Impact Levels and approval matrix:
| Level | Symptom examples | Immediate approver | Escalation needed? | Max default duration |
|-------|------------------|--------------------|--------------------|----------------------|
| P0 (Critical) | All regions > 50% error rate or core API returning 500s | Eng director + SRE lead | Exec + Legal if regulated | 24h (extendable) |
| P1 (High) | Single region large customer impact, latency > 2x SLO | On-call tech lead | Eng director if > 4h | 72h |
| P2 (Moderate) | Degraded throughput for small subset or increased tail latency | Service owner | On-call tech lead if > 8h | 7 days (rare) |

Procedure: Submitting an SLO Exception Request (SER)
1. Submit the SER using the template below (fill required fields). Attach monitoring screenshots and at least two reproducer traces if available.
2. Post a short summary to the incident bridge with the SER link.
3. Apply one of the approved temporary mitigations (see mitigation patterns) in a controlled way (canary traffic, single region, per-tenant). Do not change persistent infra configs without approval.
4. Notify customer-success for any customer-facing degradation and prepare public status page copy (see templates).
5. Re-evaluate every 30 minutes; if the mitigation is ineffective, escalate per incident playbook.

SER template (copy/paste into ticket system):
- Title: [SER] <service> - <short reason>
- Service: <service-name>
- SLO impacted: <SLA metric and target>
- Observed: <short timeline + key graphs>
- Level: P0 | P1 | P2
- Proposed mitigation: <pattern and scope (canary, tenant, region)>
- Expected outcome: <what we will recover or avoid>
- Rollback plan: <how to revert and verification steps>
- Owner: <name/email>
- Approver: <name/email>
- Evidence attachments: <links>

Approved temporary mitigation patterns (safe-by-default):
1) Traffic shaping and selective throttling
   - Apply per-tenant or per-route rate limits rather than global caps.
   - Example nginx ingress snippet (apply as canary namespace):

   apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
   kind: Ingress
   metadata:
     name: rate-limit-canary
   spec:
     annotations:
       nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-connections: "20"
       nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "50"

   Note: Always add logging headers so affected requests can be identified for rollback verification.

2) Model or variant downgrade (for model-serving services)
   - Route a small percentage of traffic to a lower-cost / lower-latency model variant with lower resource pressure.
   - Use routing policies that maintain schema compatibility (no breaking changes).

3) Regional failover or traffic reroute
   - Reroute traffic away from unhealthy region(s) using traffic manager or DNS weight shifts.
   - Maintain session affinity guarantees where required.

4) KV/prefix cache bypass or TTL reduction
   - Short-term TTL reduction to prevent cache stampede; enable pre-warming TTL path.

5) Client-side graceful degradation feature flag
   - Flip a well-tested flag to reduce feature surface (e.g., disable non-critical liveness checks, remove optional enrichment).

Mitigation safety rules:
- Limit blast radius: always scope mitigations to an environment, region, or tenant.
- Telemetry invariant: All mitigations must emit an event with mitigation-id and operator-id to the incident channel.
- Observe & verify: At least two independent telemetry signals (latency, errors, consumer success rate) must be used to decide success.
- Automatic rollback: If downstream errors increase after mitigation, revert immediately and notify approvers.

Operator checklist for applying a mitigation (10-minute procedure):
1. Confirm SER ticket exists and approver is notified.
2. Run pre-change verification: service health, SLO dashboards, top traces.
3. Apply mitigation to a narrow canary cohort (1–5% traffic or single tenant).
4. Monitor for 5 minutes across error, latency, and business metrics.
5. Gradually widen if improvement observed; otherwise roll back and escalate.
6. Update SER ticket with timestamps, canary id, and telemetry links.

Customer and status page templates:
- Internal short: "[SER] <service> - P1 - applied per-tenant throttle to reduce error rate. Monitoring: <link>. Owner: <owner>"
- External status page (public):
  Title: Service degradation for <service> in <region>
  Body: We are experiencing higher-than-normal errors for <service> in <region>. We have applied a temporary mitigation to reduce user impact while we investigate. Users may see intermittent errors or reduced feature availability. We will post updates every 60 minutes.
  What we are doing: Applying temporary traffic shaping and increasing capacity in <region>.
  ETA: We expect normal service in <hh:mm UTC> or earlier.

Evidence collection and audit (required):
- Attach: dashboard snapshots (last 60m, 6h), sample traces (10-20), alert ids, mitigation change ids, and list of affected tenants.
- Log: mitigation-id=<uuid> applied_by=<operator> at=<timestamp> scope=<canary|region|tenant>
- Post-incident: collate a 1-page evidence bundle for audits (for regulated customers).

Post-incident follow-up (within 72h):
1. Owner drafts a post-incident summary with root cause hypothesis, actions taken, evidence, and next steps (template below).
2. Assign action owners with due dates in the ticketing system.
3. Required review: SRE lead and the service owner must review and close SER with evidence of durable remediation.
4. If SER exceeded default duration or impacted regulated data, engage Legal/Compliance for record retention.

Post-incident summary template (one paragraph + bullets):
- Summary: <one-sentence incident summary and impact>
- Timeline: <hh:mm UTC> to <hh:mm UTC> key events
- Mitigation: <what was applied and why>
- Root cause: <short hypothesis or confirmed cause>
- Actions: <owner - action - due date>

Game day practice scenario (SLO exception drill):
Objective: Practice submitting SER, applying a scoped mitigation, and running evidence collection and rollback.
Roles: bridge lead, operator, service owner, SRE reviewer, customer-success observer.
Steps:
1. Inject a simulated degradation (synthetic error spike) in a staging region.
2. Operator files SER and applies canary throttling.
3. Monitor and measure effectiveness for 15 minutes.
4. If mitigation succeeds, widen and then execute rollback; otherwise escalate to Eng director.
5. Capture evidence and grade teams on time-to-SER, adherence to safety rules, and quality of customer comms.

Metrics to track for continuous improvement:
- Median time from detection to SER submission.
- Time from SER approval to mitigation applied.
- Percent of SERs that required escalation beyond first approver.
- Number of post-incident action items reopened after 30 days.

Appendix: Example curl to annotate mitigation event in incident log (replace placeholders):
curl -X POST "https://ops-api.internal.redwood/v1/mitigations" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPERATOR_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"mitigation_id":"mit-$(date +%s)","service":"<service>","scope":"canary","applied_by":"aisha.tan@redwood.com","notes":"applied per-tenant throttle during SER"}'

Governance notes:
- SERs and mitigations are retained for 12 months and are auditable.
- Repeated SERs for the same root cause must trigger a reliability review and capacity investment proposal.
- Any SER affecting regulated workloads must be reported to Compliance within 24 hours.
